customdata:
{"name": "Sun", "subtitle": "", "body": "Note: The Sun, our very own star, is a massive ball of hot plasma that sits at the center of our solar system.
It's the source of all life and energy on Earth, so I've colored it chlorophyll green in our plot!
* Type: A yellow dwarf star (G-type main-sequence star).
* Age: About 4.6 billion years old, and is expected to continue its current phase for about 5 billion years
more, then evolve into a Red Giant.
* Diameter: Roughly 1.4 million kilometers (865,000 miles), about 109 times the diameter of Earth.
* Mass: About 333,000 times the mass of Earth
* Composition: Primarily hydrogen (about 73%) and helium (about 25%), with trace amounts of other elements.
* Surface Temperature: 5778 K, around 5,500 degrees Celsius, or 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit
* Core Temperature: Around 15 million degrees Celsius (27 million degrees Fahrenheit)
* Stellar Class: Main-sequence. Stars in the prime of their lives, fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores.
* Absolute Magnitude: 4.83
* Spectral Type: G2V
* Object Type: Star
The Sun is composed of several layers:
* Core: The innermost region where nuclear fusion occurs, converting hydrogen into helium and releasing energy.
* Radiative Zone: Energy from the core travels outward through this zone via radiation.
* Convective Zone: Energy is transported through this zone via convection (the movement of hot plasma).
* Photosphere: The visible surface of the Sun.
* Chromosphere: A thin layer above the photosphere.
* Corona: The outermost layer, a very hot and tenuous plasma that extends millions of kilometers into space.
Standard for comparison to other stars:
* Luminosity: 1.000000 Lsun
* Mass: 1.00 Msun
* Distance: 0 pc (0 ly)
* Plotting marker size: 12 px"}
data.name: Sun
text:
Sun
Note: The Sun, our very own star, is a massive ball of hot plasma that sits at the center of our solar system.
It's the source of all life and energy on Earth, so I've colored it chlorophyll green in our plot!
* Type: A yellow dwarf star (G-type main-sequence star).
* Age: About 4.6 billion years old, and is expected to continue its current phase for about 5 billion years
more, then evolve into a Red Giant.
* Diameter: Roughly 1.4 million kilometers (865,000 miles), about 109 times the diameter of Earth.
* Mass: About 333,000 times the mass of Earth
* Composition: Primarily hydrogen (about 73%) and helium (about 25%), with trace amounts of other elements.
* Surface Temperature: 5778 K, around 5,500 degrees Celsius, or 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit
* Core Temperature: Around 15 million degrees Celsius (27 million degrees Fahrenheit)
* Stellar Class: Main-sequence. Stars in the prime of their lives, fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores.
* Absolute Magnitude: 4.83
* Spectral Type: G2V
* Object Type: Star
The Sun is composed of several layers:
* Core: The innermost region where nuclear fusion occurs, converting hydrogen into helium and releasing energy.
* Radiative Zone: Energy from the core travels outward through this zone via radiation.
* Convective Zone: Energy is transported through this zone via convection (the movement of hot plasma).
* Photosphere: The visible surface of the Sun.
* Chromosphere: A thin layer above the photosphere.
* Corona: The outermost layer, a very hot and tenuous plasma that extends millions of kilometers into space.
Standard for comparison to other stars:
* Luminosity: 1.000000 Lsun
* Mass: 1.00 Msun
* Distance: 0 pc (0 ly)
* Plotting marker size: 12 px

data.name: C/2025_K1: Nucleus
text:
Nucleus of C/2025_K1
Approximate size: 5 km
Cometary nuclei are 'dirty snowballs' - irregular chunks of ice, rock, and dust.
As they approach the Sun, surface ice sublimates, releasing gas and dust.
Note: The nucleus is far too small to show at scale with the coma.

_encyclopedia.Sun:
Horizons: 10. The star at the center of our solar system. To display structure and atmosphere select "Solar Shells".

* Missions:
  * Pioneer 5 (NASA/DOD, 1960): Measured magnetic field phenomena, solar flare particles, and ionization.
  * Helios 1 & 2 (DFVLR/NASA, 1974 & 1976): Studied solar wind, magnetic and electric fields, cosmic rays, and dust.
  * ISEE-3 (NASA, 1978): Observed solar phenomena in conjunction with Earth-orbiting satellites, comets.
  * Ulysses (ESA/NASA, 1990-2009): Observed the Sun's polar regions and the solar wind at high solar latitudes.
  * WIND (NASA, 1994-Present): Still active, it provides continuous measurements of the solar wind.
  * SOHO (Solar and Heliospheric Observatory) (ESA/NASA, 1995-Present): A continuous view from its core to the solar wind.
  * ACE (Advanced Composition Explorer) (NASA, 1997-Present): Measures particles from the solar wind and galactic cosmic rays.
  * Hinode (JAXA/NASA/ESA/STFC, 2006-Present): Explores the Sun's magnetic fields.
  * STEREO (Solar TErrestrial RElations Observatory) (NASA, 2006-Present): Imaging the 3D structure of coronal mass ejections.
  * Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) (NASA, 2010-Present): High-resolution images of solar flares and eruptions.
  * IRIS (Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph) (NASA, 2013-Present): Sun's lower atmosphere (chromosphere and transition).
  * Parker Solar Probe (NASA, 2018-Present): Flew through the corona to study coronal heating and solar wind acceleration.
  * Solar Orbiter (ESA/NASA, 2020-Present): Provides unprecedented insight into how our local star "works" with 10 science instruments.
  * PUNCH (Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere) (NASA, Launched March 2025): Will study the Sun's outer atmosphere.
  * Solar Polar Orbit Observatory (Planned 2029): Will study views of its polar regions.
_encyclopedia.C/2025_K1:
Horizons: C/2025 K1. Retrograde > 90. Comet C/2025 K1 (ATLAS) is a recently discovered comet that is expected to become a notable object for 
observation in late 2025. Here's a breakdown of what we know:
* Discovery and Classification: It was discovered on May 25, 2025, by the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System (ATLAS) 
  survey in Chile. It appears to be a dynamically new comet, meaning it's likely making its first close passage to the Sun.
* Orbital Characteristics: Perihelion (closest approach to the Sun): October 8, 2025, at a distance of approximately 0.33 AU, 
  which is closer than Mercury's orbit. This close approach to the Sun is significant and could lead to substantial brightening.
* Closest approach to Earth: November 24, 2025, at a distance of about 0.40 AU.
* Eccentricity (e): The orbit is highly eccentric, 1.000251464554613 (July 11, 2025), indicating an unbound or nearly parabolic orbit.
* Inclination (i): The orbital plane is highly inclined, 147.864867556013 degrees.
* Fragmentation: Nucleus fragmented ~October 16, 2025, approximately 8 days after perihelion at 0.33 AU
  (inside Mercury's orbit). Hubble Space Telescope observed at least 4 fragments, each with a distinct coma,
  on Nov 8-10, 2025 (published Icarus, Feb 2026, Auburn University). This is Fragment A (main body).
  Fragment C is unique: e=0.99999 (gravitationally bound, ~13 million year return) while B and D escape.
* Visibility and Brightness: As of early July 2025, it's around magnitude 14-15, requiring a telescope for observation.
* Predicted Peak Brightness: It's expected to brighten significantly as it approaches perihelion. Predictions suggest it could 
  reach a magnitude of around 5.2 to 8 in early October 2025.
* Naked-eye visibility: While magnitude 5.2 is generally considered within naked-eye visibility under very dark skies, it's 
  more likely to be a binocular object for most observers, especially at its peak brightness.
* Observing Locations: Early October (near perihelion), observers in northern latitudes will see it best in the morning sky. 
  Observers in southern latitudes can spot it in both the evening and morning skies.
* August: It will be faint (around magnitude 13) and visible only from the Southern Hemisphere through large telescopes.
* VISUALIZATION NOTE: Fragment trajectories are backward-extrapolated from post-breakup observations
  (Nov 2025 - Jan 2026). Apparent separation at perihelion (Oct 8) is a computational artifact -
  the comet was still intact at that date. Fragments never converge to zero because the parent orbit
  includes non-gravitational forces (CO2 outgassing) while fragment orbits do not. The minimum
  cluster size (~70,000 km) occurs around Nov 25, well after the actual breakup.
_encyclopedia.C/2025_K1-D:
Horizons: C/2025 K1-D. Fragment D of comet C/2025 K1 (ATLAS).
* One of four fragments observed by Hubble Space Telescope in November 2025 (published Icarus, Feb 2026).
* The most divergent fragment - highest eccentricity (e=1.00246) of all four pieces.
* Also the faintest and least observed, with the shortest data arc (33 days).
* Perihelion: October 8.46, 2025, at 0.336 AU.
* By March 2026, Fragment D leads the divergence at ~911,000 km from Fragment A.
* No non-gravitational forces modeled.
* Data arc: 2025-11-26 to 2025-12-29 (107 observations, JPL solution #5).
* VISUALIZATION NOTE: Plotted position at perihelion is backward-extrapolated from
  post-breakup observations. The comet was still intact on Oct 8; breakup occurred ~Oct 16.
_encyclopedia.C/2025_K1-C:
Horizons: C/2025 K1-C. Fragment C of comet C/2025 K1 (ATLAS) - the stubborn one.
* The ONLY fragment that remains gravitationally bound to the Sun (e=0.99999).
* While fragments A, B, and D escape the solar system on hyperbolic orbits,
  Fragment C is on an extremely long-period elliptical orbit (~13 million years).
* Its orbital elements are closest to the parent body, suggesting it may be
  the most massive fragment or the one least affected by outgassing forces.
* Perihelion: October 8.44, 2025, at 0.334 AU.
* Chemically unusual: ground-based observations show extreme depletion of carbon-bearing species.
* Data arc: 2025-11-25 to 2026-01-10 (158 observations, JPL solution #14).
